source.title: What We Talk About When We Talk About LLM Planning: Evidence for Two Distinct Planning Abilities
source.authors: Sukai Huang; Chenyuan Zhang; Fu-Cai Ke; Zhixi Cai; Naim Rastgoo; G. Haffari; Hamid Rezatofighi

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or document mismatch; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether downstream planning performance varies with model scale, using IRT-derived competency estimates rather than held-out cross-entropy loss or the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper measures planning performance across model sizes and inference conditions, so it bears on V6. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, test large-run extrapolation, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. References to scaling laws and other studies are not treated as results from this study.
record.test_reason: The study regresses IRT-estimated planning ability of off-the-shelf models (0.8B–27B, three families) on log parameter count. This is a downstream-performance-vs-scale result in a new setting (symbolic planning, ACPBench-Hard), so it bears on V6. It does not measure pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, or study compute allocation or architecture shape.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that LLM planning on ACPBench-Hard decomposes into two non-compensatory competencies. Operational reasoning improves with model size and CoT; structural enumeration stays flat across sizes and inference budgets, and scaffolds can lower it. Closing the gap likely needs interventions beyond scaling. They caution that the scale regressions are pooled, non-causal associations and that model coverage stops at 27B open-weight models.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates planning-benchmark accuracy through IRT-derived latent competencies and a regression on model size; it does not measure held-out cross-entropy or fit the original scaling-law curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported regression includes inference-condition indicators and model-family indicators. The paper also reports that prompting and scaffolding affect the two latent dimensions differently.

fits_no_version.finding: CoT and agent-scaffold (test-time compute) raise operational ability (+1.81, +1.97) but lower structural ability (−0.39, −1.19) relative to Direct.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time reasoning budget improves some downstream competencies but not others (inference-time scaling, not pretraining scale).

fits_no_version.finding: Linear-probe decoding of item difficulty from hidden states strengthens with model size (joint MSE 3.29 at 9B vs 2.72 at 27B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Internal representation of task difficulty becomes more decodable with scale.

record.problems: The scale relationships are pooled associations, not causal estimates. The authors note limits in model coverage and that they did not evaluate proprietary systems; the paper also does not report uncertainty for the scale-regression coefficients or test predictive generalization of those relationships.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results left out. Other results concern IRT model selection, prompting, answer formats, interventions, probes, and routing rather than the versions tested here.

untested.parts: Whether downstream gains are predictable (out-of-sample extrapolation to larger models); relation of performance to pretraining loss; scales beyond 27B; proprietary models.

missing.what: Within-family scale trajectories (Qwen3.5 0.8B–27B sweep; Gemma 4 E2B–12B; Granite 3.3 2B–8B) showing θ1 rising and θ2 flat. Shown only as figures, no per-family coefficients.

record.verdict_notes: V6 evidence is incidental to the paper's main aim of identifying latent dimensions. The scale range is narrow (~1.5 orders of magnitude) and pooled across families with different training. The ability measure is an IRT latent from a joint calibration, so V6 bears on it only indirectly. The CoT/scratchpad coefficients concern inference-time compute, not pretraining scale, so they are not linked to V6.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their trends with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study evaluates planning performance against model size, but does not test performance against pretraining loss or validate out-of-sample predictions of downstream performance.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and departures of loss curves from power laws.

rows.size_stated: Qwen3.5 0.8B–27B; Qwen3.8 27B; Gemma 4 E2B, E4B, 12B; Granite 3.3 2B, 8B
rows.operation_detail: Regressed IRT-derived operational ability on centered log model size, controlling for model family and inference condition.

conditions.value: Direct, CoT, and Scratchpad; Direct is the reference condition
Pooled model–condition pairs across model families

rows.measure: Regression coefficient for centered log model size on IRT ability
rows.note: The paper says operational ability increases with model size. The authors caution that these pooled associations are not causal estimates.
rows.check: Value +4.34 is correct (Table 11). The measure is a latent IRT ability, not raw task accuracy; the reference condition is Direct. The §I equation lists only size and condition predictors, but the §J.2 latent regression adds family indicators, so the record's 'controlling for model family' is ambiguous. No uncertainty is reported for the coefficient.

rows.operation_detail: Regressed IRT-derived structural ability on centered log model size, controlling for model family and inference condition.

conditions.value: Direct, CoT, and Scratchpad; Direct is the reference condition
Pooled model–condition pairs across model families

rows.measure: Regression coefficient for centered log model size on IRT ability
rows.note: The authors describe this as showing no comparable positive effect and say structural enumeration remains flat across model sizes.
rows.check: Value +0.07 is correct; the authors call it 'no comparable positive effect'. No uncertainty is reported. Dimension 2 is partly at floor: areach b2=+3.63 is near floor for nearly all respondents, which may limit sensitivity to scale gains.

relationships.condition: Operational-reasoning planning tasks (app, prog, val, nexta), pooled across Qwen/Gemma/Granite and inference conditions, 0.8B–27B
relationships.reason: Operational IRT ability rises with log model size (coefficient +4.34; r1). Per-family trajectories (Figs 7–9) agree. The association is pooled, non-causal, and reported without CIs.
relationships.display_finding: Operational IRT ability rises with log model size with coefficient +4.34, consistent with individual family trajectories, although the pooled association is non-causal and lacks confidence intervals.

relationships.condition: Structural-enumeration planning tasks (reach, land, areach), same models and conditions
relationships.reason: Structural IRT ability shows essentially no size effect (+0.07; r2), and the authors state it stays flat across sizes. Floor effects on the hardest items may contribute.
relationships.display_finding: The structural IRT ability size effect was only +0.07, with floor effects on the hardest items potentially contributing to the flat trend.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
